claims.text: A W-based WxTaTiVCr-like refractory high-entropy alloy can be fabricated by powder metallurgy followed by spark plasma sintering at approximately 1600 °C.
Controlled Ti and trace-carbon additions during this process will cause in situ TiC precipitation.
The in situ TiC precipitates will be nanoscale, finely dispersed, and uniformly distributed.
The alloy matrix containing the TiC precipitates is BCC.
Nano-TiC particles are stable sinks for radiation-induced point defects.
Nano-TiC particles capture and annihilate radiation-induced point defects.
Defect capture and annihilation by TiC will reduce irradiation-induced defect accumulation and swelling.
In situ TiC contributes dispersion strengthening in the W-based alloy.
The TiC-containing alloy will have improved hardness and strength.
Dispersion strengthening by TiC will improve hardness and yield strength without compromising ductility.
Under simulated fusion-relevant irradiation, the Ti-modified alloy will exhibit less swelling and lower defect density than the unmodified alloy.
Under simulated fusion-relevant irradiation, the Ti-modified alloy will exhibit higher hardness and strength than the unmodified alloy.
Departing from the specified sintering conditions or controlled Ti/C levels may compromise TiC formation, homogeneity, or stability.
Inhomogeneous TiC distributions could produce variable defect-sink efficiency or localized embrittlement.
A baseline WxTaTiVCr-like alloy produced without intentional Ti addition will not form the proposed in situ TiC precipitates.

contradictions.description: The initial and baseline material is described as compositionally similar to WxTaTiVCr, which already contains Ti, while the intervention and baseline contrast are framed as introducing intentional Ti versus having no intentional Ti addition. The actual compositional difference between baseline and modified samples is therefore internally ambiguous.
